In 1494, two kingdoms sat down and drew a line down the Atlantic Ocean.

West of it: Spain. East of it: Portugal.

Nobody asked the millions of people already living in what they were dividing.

The treaty that split the world — a thread 🧵🗺️

1/ The trigger: Columbus. His 1492 voyage for Spain threatened Portugal's decades-old monopoly on new lands, granted by the Pope in 1481. Lisbon panicked — could Spain just sail west and claim everything?
2/ Pope Alexander VI, a Spaniard by birth, drew the first line in 1493: 100 leagues west of Cape Verde. Portugal's king looked at it and said: not far enough. Move it west.
3/ The two crowns negotiated directly and signed at Tordesillas on June 7, 1494, sliding the line to 370 leagues west of Cape Verde. Nobody involved had actually seen what was out there yet.

4/ That renegotiation is the entire reason Brazil speaks Portuguese today. The new line happened to slice through South America's unmapped eastern bulge — 6 years before a Portuguese fleet confirmed it existed.

5/ France's king reportedly demanded to see the clause in 'Adam's will' excluding him from the New World. Non-signatories just ignored the line — French, English and Dutch ships spent the next century seizing Iberian cargo and grabbing colonies of their own.

6/ The line couldn't even survive contact with the rest of the globe. A second treaty, at Zaragoza in 1529, had to draw a matching line on the OTHER side of the world — and it still left years of disputed overlap in the Philippines.

Full story — the Pope, the panic, and how one redrawn meridian still shapes where Portuguese is spoken today — in this week's Lines & Legends, free every 3 days: https://buttondown.com/forummapping
